title: WHY DO CHRISTIANS SOMETIMES PRAY MORE THAN THEY OBEY?
paragraphs: WHY DO CHRISTIANS SOMETIMES PRAY MORE THAN THEY OBEY?
There is a kind of prayer that fills churches but never reaches the battlefield.
Some of the most heartbreaking words in Scripture are not spoken to atheists.
They are spoken to people who knew how to pray.
People who sincerely believed they were close to God.
Yet Jesus looked directly at them and said:
"Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?" (Luke 6:46)
The issue was never that they lacked prayer.
The issue was that they lacked surrender.
Many Christians today are not struggling because they pray too little.
They are struggling because they pray about things they already know they should obey.
The prayer closet has become a waiting room for delayed obedience.
And delayed obedience has always been one of Satan's favorite victories.
The kind that keeps praying while refusing to move.
It is possible to spend hours talking to God while ignoring what He already said.
That realization should shake every one of us.
Because if we are honest, we have all done it.
We have prayed for courage while avoiding the conversation.
Prayed for guidance while ignoring the conviction.
Prayed for breakthrough while refusing forgiveness.
Prayed for healing while protecting the sin that keeps wounding us.
Prayed for revival while neglecting repentance.
And somehow we convinced ourselves that talking about obedience was the same thing as obedience itself.
The ancient Hebrew understanding helps us see something we often miss.
The Hebrew word often associated with hearing is שָׁמַע (Shama).
But Shama does not simply mean hearing sounds.
It carries the idea of hearing with the intention of responding.
To hear God was to obey God.
The ancient Hebrew mind did not separate listening from action.
The command was not merely to listen.
To align life with what had been heard.
In Scripture, hearing without obedience was considered a failure to hear at all.
That should stop us in our tracks.
Because modern Christianity often celebrates information.
One can memorize verses and still resist God.
One can quote theology and still avoid surrender.
One can lead prayers and still refuse obedience.
Jesus exposed this reality through one of the most uncomfortable teachings in the New Testament.
The Greek text of Matthew 7:21 records Him saying:
"Οὐ πᾶς ὁ λέγων μοι· Κύριε Κύριε"
"Not everyone who says to Me, 'Lord, Lord'..."
The problem was not what they called Him.
The problem was that their confession never became submission.
"...but the one who does the will of My Father who is in heaven."
The Greek word translated "does" is ποιῶν (poiōn).
Jesus never taught that salvation is earned by works.
Scripture repeatedly affirms salvation by grace through faith.
But genuine faith inevitably produces obedience.
Obedience is not the root of salvation.
When the fruit is completely absent, the tree must be examined.
This is where many believers become uncomfortable.
Because prayer can sometimes feel easier than obedience.
Prayer allows us to remain in control.
Obedience forces us to surrender control.
Prayer allows us to imagine possibilities.
Obedience often costs us something publicly.
And movement is where fear becomes visible.
There came a moment when another prayer meeting was not required.
At some point Abraham had to stop praying about the call and start walking toward it.
The miracle was not in the discussion.
The miracle was in the obedience.
The same pattern appears throughout Scripture.
Peter stepped out of the boat.
And history changed when somebody obeyed.
Perhaps that is why James writes with such urgency:
The Greek term ποιηταὶ (poiētai) means doers, practitioners, performers.
People who embody what they believe.
Self-deception is easier than open rebellion.
The rebel knows he is resisting God.
The self-deceived believer often thinks he is obeying while doing nothing.
That may be one of the greatest spiritual dangers in the modern church.
We mistake emotional conviction for transformation.
And then we wonder why spiritual growth feels stalled.
Many times we are resisting the last instruction He already gave.
The next breakthrough often hides behind the last command.
The next season often waits beyond the last act of obedience.
The next miracle often begins where excuses end.
Perhaps there is someone reading this who already knows exactly what God has been asking.
You know the relationship that needs forgiveness.
You know the secret sin that needs confession.
You know the habit that needs surrender.
You know the ministry He keeps calling you toward.
You know the step of faith you keep postponing.
And that knowledge is precisely why this article feels uncomfortable.
Because deep down, the Holy Spirit is not asking for another debate.
The Aramaic language spoken by Jesus carried a profound understanding of lordship.
When believers confessed Jesus as "Maran" (Lord), they were not merely acknowledging a title.
And yet every command He gives is rooted in love.
Every instruction is aimed at life.
Every act of surrender is leading us toward freedom.
The commands of God are not chains.
The irony is that obedience often feels dangerous right before it becomes beautiful.
Ask anyone who has ever followed Jesus beyond comfort.
Faith has always walked before sight.
Maybe that is why Jesus never said:
"If you love Me, feel deeply about Me."
"If you love Me, keep My commandments." (John 14:15)
Love that never obeys is not biblical love.
And perhaps that is the question echoing through this moment.
Not whether you posted Scripture online.
Because sometimes the most spiritual thing you can do is stop asking God for another sign and start obeying the instruction He already gave.
Your honesty may encourage someone else who feels alone in the struggle.
One day we will discover that the prayers that changed our lives were often answered through the obedience we kept postponing.
